summary: Specifies the ARPANET Short Blocking Feature, which lets hosts shorten the IMP's host blocking timer. It replaces a never-implemented non-blocking interface.

plainLanguage.summary: When the network is busy it tells a computer to wait. This feature lets the computer choose a shorter wait.

questions: what is the arpanet short blocking feature
why do network hosts get blocked
how does short blocking timeout work
what rejection codes mean in arpanet
subtitle: Letting ARPANET hosts escape long blocking timeouts.

tldr.problem: When a host sends a message to an ARPANET IMP, the IMP could block (refuse new messages) for up to 15 seconds while gathering resources, even if the host has other messages that could be processed immediately.
tldr.mechanism: The Short Blocking Feature introduces message subtypes that allow hosts to request a maximum 2-second block timeout instead of 15 seconds. If the message cannot be processed within 2 seconds, the IMP rejects it with a reason code, allowing the host to submit other messages in the meantime.
tldr.outcome: Hosts gain better control over their blocking behavior and can work around resource contention by submitting messages adaptively, though they must handle rejection and resubmission.

today: RFC 852 is Historic. The ARPANET itself ceased operations in 1990, replaced by the Internet and its TCP/IP protocols. Short Blocking was a pragmatic solution for managing resource contention in an earlier packet-switched network; modern IP-based networks use congestion control and backpressure mechanisms instead.

sections.title: The Blocking Problem on ARPANET
sections.content:
The ARPANET uses Interface Message Processors (IMPs) to handle communication between hosts. When a host submits a message to its IMP, the IMP must allocate resources (buffers, routing tables, connection state) before transmitting it. If these resources are not available, the IMP blocks the host—stops accepting further messages from that host—until resources are freed.

In the original design, blocking could last up to 15 seconds. This creates a fairness problem: a host may have multiple messages queued, some of which require few resources and could be processed immediately, but all are delayed because the IMP is blocked waiting for resources for a single heavy message.

The Short Blocking Feature replaces the never-implemented non-blocking interface with a practical option for shorter timeouts, available on C/30 IMPs using either 1822 or 1822L host access protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMP is like a post office sorting machine. When one package needs special handling, the whole machine stops until that's done. Short Blocking lets you say: 'If you can't sort this package in 2 seconds, put it aside and handle the next one.'

sections.title: Message Subtypes for Blocking Control
sections.content:
Type 0 (Regular) messages now have four subtypes, differing in blocking behavior and error handling:

Subtype 0 (Standard) instructs the IMP to use its full message and error control facilities, with blocking lasting up to 15 seconds.

Subtype 1 (Standard, Short Blocking) requests the same facilities as subtype 0 but limits blocking to a maximum of 2 seconds. If the message cannot be processed within that time, the IMP sends a Type 9 (Incomplete Transmission) rejection.

Subtype 3 (Uncontrolled Packet) disables message control and delivery guarantees, blocking for up to 15 seconds though actual blockage is unlikely.

Subtype 4 (Uncontrolled, Short Blocking) combines uncontrolled transmission with a 2-second maximum blocking time.

Hosts using short blocking subtypes must be prepared to handle Type 9 rejection messages and resubmit messages that time out.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the post office machine: 'Quick mode, standard service, 2 seconds or reject it' or 'Quick mode, no guarantee, 2 seconds or skip it.' This gives hosts more control.

sections.title: Why Messages Get Rejected
sections.content:
When a message is rejected, the IMP returns a Type 9 (Incomplete Transmission) message with a subtype code indicating the reason. Subtypes 0–5 apply to all messages. For short blocking messages specifically, subtypes 6–10 describe why the 2-second timeout was exceeded.

Connection set-up delay (subtype 6) occurs when the IMP needs to establish or reuse a virtual circuit connection to the destination, causing a delay. Other messages for different destinations can still be accepted.

End-to-end flow control (subtype 7) is the most common cause: the ARPANET limits each connection to eight outstanding messages. If all eight slots are full, a ninth message is rejected; however, messages to other destinations can proceed.

Destination IMP buffer shortage (subtype 8) happens when the destination IMP has insufficient buffer space for messages over 1008 bits. Smaller messages or messages to other connections may still be accepted.

Congestion control (subtype 9) rejects a message when the path to the destination is overloaded, but messages to other destinations may be acceptable.

Local resource shortage (subtype 10) indicates the source IMP itself lacks buffers or tables to accept any message.
sections.plainLanguage: The rejection codes tell the host why it failed: connection setup taking too long, the recipient is slow, the destination is full, the path is crowded, or the source is out of resources. Each suggests a different fix.

sections.title: Sequential Delivery Tradeoff
sections.content:
Short blocking introduces a subtle but important limitation: the order in which messages are accepted by the IMP may not match the order in which the host submitted them. This occurs because messages that time out are rejected while other messages submitted later may be accepted immediately.

The ARPANET normally provides sequential delivery—messages with the same priority, source, and destination are delivered in submission order. When a host uses short blocking, this guarantee breaks down: if message A is rejected and message B (submitted after A) is accepted, the receiving host may see B before A.

This tradeoff is acceptable for applications that do not require ordered delivery but unacceptable for those that do. The RFC advises that applications requiring sequential delivery should not use short blocking.
sections.plainLanguage: Because rejected messages go back to the queue and submitted messages jump ahead, they can arrive out of order. It's like cutting in line and then going to the back—things get out of sequence.
